name: Dal Baati Churma
excerpt: Three dishes, one plate — the complete meal of Rajasthan. The baati was originally baked in the embers of a soldiers' camp fire.
body:
Dal Baati Churma is the food of a harsh geography. Rajasthan is not gentle — the desert takes water, and cooking methods adapted to what fire could do that water could not.

Baati is a dense wheat ball baked in the embers of a fire. It does not need water during cooking — it bakes dry, until a hard crust forms. When done, it is split open, drenched in clarified butter, and placed beside the dal.

The dal is slow-cooked with five lentils (panch mel dal), tempered with ghee, spices, and dried mango powder. The churma is the sweet counterpoint — coarsely ground wheat, fried and mixed with jaggery and ghee.

Together, they form a meal that could sustain a Rajput warrior on a long march. In Jaipur today, it is eaten at weddings, at festivals, and at restaurants where the fire-baking is maintained as discipline — not nostalgia.

"My grandmother made baati in a wood fire for seventy years," says the owner of a Jaipur dhaba. "She said gas baati has no soul. I don't know if I agree. But I still use wood."
